metadata.subtitle: One Record, Different Lines

beats.narration_text: Hear "Claude has an investigation-summary skill" and your brain fills in one write-up — one document, handed to whoever asks. That's the picture the name pushes, and it's the wrong one.

Here's why that fails. The investigation is privileged, and not every reader is entitled to the same amount of it. Send outside counsel's version to the workforce and you've handed over the exact analysis the privilege exists to protect. One summary optimizes for uniformity at the expense of the boundary that makes the record legally safe to hold.

shot.new_visual_element: NOT EVERYONE IS OWED THE SAME

production_viz.label: NOT EVERYONE IS OWED THE SAME
production_viz.caption: privilege breaks first

beats.narration_text: Here's what the skill actually is — one file. investigation-summary is a folder holding a single SKILL.md: plain-language instructions Claude reads before it drafts anything, telling it how to write an audience-specific summary from one underlying privileged investigation. No code, no branching in the engine — the choices live in the prose.

The machinery is boring on purpose. Claude reads that file top to bottom, then works through it in order: read the investigation record, draft for the audience it's told to draft for, return that one output. No branching, unless the file itself says branch.

That makes it a specification, not judgment about privilege. They optimized for predictability at the expense of judgment. The payoff: the same audience gets the same shape of summary, every run — reviewable, auditable. The limit: a reader the file never anticipated gets no guidance on where the line should sit. The file is the whole policy; if it doesn't cover a case, nothing does.

So investigation-summary never writes "the" summary of an investigation. It writes one summary, once per audience, drawn from the same privileged record each time. The file — not the reader, not Claude in the moment — decides where the line falls.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — ONE FILE, MANY LINES

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — ONE FILE, MANY LINES
production_viz.caption: same file, a different line each time

beats.narration_text: The output doesn't audit itself. A summary that reads as plain fact doesn't prove privileged material was stripped — the case might have had little to redact in the first place. A summary that withholds a lot doesn't prove the boundary was drawn right — it might have cut more, or less, than that audience was owed. This works if you value the file's decisions holding across runs; it fails if you need the artifact to certify its own privilege.

production_viz.label: NEITHER ONE IS PROOF
production_viz.caption: neither proves the line was drawn right

beats.narration_text: investigation-summary never hands out one summary of an investigation. It draws a different line for each audience from the same privileged record — so what one reader sees is never a safe stand-in for what another gets.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I have one document from work I need to send to two different audiences — I'll describe both. For each audience, draft me a SKILL.md-style instruction file: what to include verbatim, what to summarize, what to withhold, and one sentence of reasoning per rule. Then, before writing either summary, read the two files back to me and name one question you'd need answered to draw the lines better. Go deeper: what would change in those instructions if a third audience showed up next month that neither file anticipated — and how would you know the existing files couldn't handle them?

llm_exercise.prompt: I have one document from work I need to send to two different audiences. I'll describe the document in one paragraph, then audience A and audience B in one paragraph each. For each audience, draft me a SKILL.md-style instruction file that Claude could follow later: what to include verbatim, what to summarize, what to withhold entirely, and one sentence of reasoning per rule. Before writing either summary, read the two files back to me and name one question you'd need me to answer to draw the lines better.
